extracted.intended_audience: lawyers, patent practitioners, inventors, and scholars interested in English patent law (early 19th century)
extracted.subtask_description: Guidance and legal standards for obtaining, drafting, enforcing, and defending letters patent in England (includes patentability, specification drafting, procedural practice, and litigation/remedies). Applicable to practitioners advising inventors and patentees circa 1832.

rubrics_metrics.name: Newness of the invention (novelty)
rubrics_metrics.description: It is essential that it be new.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A 'new manufacture' must not have been before published or used; novelty is destroyed by prior publication or prior sale/use. The thing claimed must not be copied from a scientific book or suggested by others. Where the thing claimed is not new but some other part of the manufacture is, the new part may be protected (see distinctions in cases).

rubrics_metrics.name: No prior use by others or inventor
rubrics_metrics.description: Not used before — neither (1) by others, — nor (2) by the inventor.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Prior use by even a few persons, or making and selling before patent, can destroy novelty. Use by the inventor before obtaining the patent (even for experiments) may bar the patent; four months' use is noted as problematic and may be doubtful even for experiments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Vendibility
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be vendible.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The subject of a patent must be capable of being sold (vendible matter); mere curiosities not vendible will not qualify.

rubrics_metrics.name: Material and useful (utility requirement)
rubrics_metrics.description: The invention must be material and useful.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patentable manufacture must have practical utility demonstrated by experiments; trivial alterations or mere curiosities without utility are not patentable.

rubrics_metrics.name: Types of patentable subjects (what counts as a 'new manufacture')
rubrics_metrics.description: A new manufacture may be: (I) a substance or thing made; (II) a machine or instrument; (III) an improvement or addition; (IV) a combination or arrangement of things already known; (V) a principle, method, or process carried into practice by tangible means; (VI) a chemical discovery; (VII) a foreign invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise distinguishes each type and provides tailored specification and novelty considerations. Notably: abstract principles alone are not patentable; methods/processes are patentable only when carried into effect by something material and tangible.

rubrics_metrics.name: Abstract principles not patentable
rubrics_metrics.description: An abstract principle cannot be a new manufacture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The application or practice of a principle, without tangible means, is not patentable. Patents for methods/processes are acceptable only when subject to something material and tangible (e.g., apparatus or tangible steps).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification requirement (existence and nature)
rubrics_metrics.description: A specification is required and has general properties and a particular nature.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification is not prescribed by the statute but is inserted in the patent; it must accurately ascertain the invention, connect with the patent, and describe the invention according to its kind (substance, machine, improvement, combination, method, chemical discovery, foreign invention).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification must enable practical replication
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must be such that a common mechanic can make it without experiments or reference to scientific books.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification should enable a person skilled in the art to make the invention from the description alone; omission of necessary descriptions renders the specification insufficient and may void the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Title must correspond with specification
rubrics_metrics.description: The title of the patent must correspond with the description in the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Claims in the title should neither be excessively extensive nor overly confined. Claiming one thing when another is really meant can vitiate the patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claims must not appropriate old parts (originality of claimed parts)
rubrics_metrics.description: Parts claimed must be original; must not, even unintentionally, appropriate any part that is old.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A specification should not claim old subject-matter as new. Describing old parts need not be unnecessary, but appropriating known features as new is incorrect and can invalidate claims.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoiding ambiguity in specification terms
rubrics_metrics.description: The terms of a specification must not be ambiguous.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ambiguous language in the specification may generally render the patent void. Use of generic terms where a particular species is intended, or misuse of technical words, produces uncertainty; technical language must be used carefully and clearly.

rubrics_metrics.name: Inclusion only of necessary descriptions; avoid misleading or useless matter
rubrics_metrics.description: Necessary descriptions must not be omitted; useless parts must not be put in to mislead.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Every material new part must be described; inserting unnecessary or misleading components (including parts that the patentee never used) may render the specification incorrect and the patent void.

rubrics_metrics.name: Correctness and sufficiency of drawings
rubrics_metrics.description: Drawings must be correct (preferably to scale); incorrect drawings can vitiate the patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Drawings are not a substitute for an adequate description and must accurately represent the invention. Failure to draw to scale or incorrect figures may contribute to invalidity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Multiple modes/ways and multiple effects: risk of partial failure
rubrics_metrics.description: If one of different ways or different ingredients named fails, or one of several effects specified is not produced, the patent may be void.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specifying several independent modes or effects and having some fail can undermine the specification's sufficiency; drafts should avoid presenting alternative ways as essential when they may not all work.

rubrics_metrics.name: Specification signing, acknowledgement and enrolment formalities
rubrics_metrics.description: Specification must be under the hands and seal of the inventor, acknowledged by a Master in Chancery, and enrolled; there is a time allowed to enrol it and a certificate of enrolment.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Failure to enrol within the allowed time leads to prescribed consequences (petition de novo, etc.). Inspection and certificate procedures are statutory/formal steps to secure the patent's validity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Connection between patent and specification
rubrics_metrics.description: There is a strict connection of the patent and specification; title and specification must correspond.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: A patent's scope is tethered to its specification; discrepancies between the patent's title/claims and the specification invite invalidation or narrow construction.

rubrics_metrics.name: What makes a patent void (general grounds)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents can be void generally when: contrary to law, mischievous to the state, not the inventor, subject not proper, insufficient specification, not obtained in the usual manner.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The statutory and common-law limits (including the Statute of Monopolies) provide multiple grounds for invalidity: policy-based grounds (injurious to trade/state), formal defects, and substantive defects (lack of novelty/utility/adequacy).

rubrics_metrics.name: Specific statutory policy constraints (Statute of Monopolies)
rubrics_metrics.description: Patents are permitted by 21 Jac. I. for certain periods and subject to policy limits; the statute confines grants to new inventions and regulates the specification condition.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The construction of the statute should favour public interest; there is no right to demand a patent and statutory clauses limit what may be granted (e.g., not for nuisance or things hurtful to trade).

rubrics_metrics.name: Inventor identity and standing
rubrics_metrics.description: An 'inventor' may be a discoverer, a first publisher, or an introducer of a foreign invention; not he who has not formed the original idea himself, taken it from a scientific work, or been merely informed of the secret.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The plaintiff must prove inventor status in infringement suits. Information obtained via servant or through fraud affects entitlement; first publication or first introduction can confer inventorship rights in some circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Prior publication and secrecy rules
rubrics_metrics.description: Publication prior to the patent destroys novelty; secret inventions are not protected by the law (no right in secret inventions).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Knowledge of a secret without publication does not count as 'use', but making it public or selling will destroy novelty; the law does not protect mere secrets—publicity is critical to establish rights via patent.

rubrics_metrics.name: Public use and experiment exceptions (narrow)
rubrics_metrics.description: Use for experiments and certain short pre-patent uses are discussed but may be doubtful; inventor's prior use even for experiments may bar patent.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise warns that use by the inventor prior to patent, even for experiments, is risky and may negate novelty; guidance is conservative—avoid public exploitation before filing.

rubrics_metrics.name: Patentable improvements & how to specify them
rubrics_metrics.description: An improvement or addition may be patented; the specification should describe the addition and how it is applied to old parts or describe the whole and distinguish the new parts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: It's not always necessary to describe old parts in detail; different ways exist to specify improvements: (a) describe only the addition and its application, or (b) describe the entire construct but distinguish the new elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Combination patents (union of two or more machines/articles)
rubrics_metrics.description: Combinations or arrangements of known things may be patentable; specifications must show that parts are united and the operation of the combination.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When patenting a combination, the specification must explain how the parts operate together and, where old combinations are claimed, must show novelty in the particular arrangement or resulting function.

rubrics_metrics.name: Method/process specifications and limits
rubrics_metrics.description: Methods/processes are considered; a mere method may be problematic unless carried into effect by tangible means.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise examines Watt's steam engine case: patents for mere methods without material apparatus are limited; to be patentable a process usually needs some material embodiment or stepwise tangible implementation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Chemical discovery standards
rubrics_metrics.description: Special rules for chemical discoveries are provided (specification form and sufficiency).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Chemical discoveries must be adequately described so that a skilled practitioner can reproduce them; the peculiarities of chemical specification and demonstration of utility are emphasized.

rubrics_metrics.name: Foreign inventions and introducers
rubrics_metrics.description: Introducer of a foreign invention can be inventor within meaning of statute; foreign inventions have particular practice rules.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The specification and practice for foreign inventions are treated separately; introducing a foreign invention may confer rights if the introducer is the first to publish or apply it locally.

rubrics_metrics.name: Practice of obtaining a patent (procedural instruments)
rubrics_metrics.description: Procedure includes: petition and affidavit, the Attorney‑General's report, the bill for the patent, King's warrant, sign manual, signet, privy seal, the patent and the specification, enrolment, certificate of enrolment, and inspection of the specification.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Each instrument and step has legal and practical import; the bill issues and is progressed through the prerogative/formal offices, and the specification must be enrolled in Chancery within prescribed time to complete formalities.

rubrics_metrics.name: Enrolment and inspection formalities and timelines
rubrics_metrics.description: Time allowed to enrol the specification; certificate of enrolment; inspection of the specification and occasional statutory limitations (inspection only by Lord Chancellor).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Enrolment is essential to complete the patent's formal life; failure to enrol or to comply with inspection provisions can lead to loss of rights or need for a fresh petition.

rubrics_metrics.name: Grounds and procedure for repealing patents (scire facias)
rubrics_metrics.description: Proceedings by scire facias to repeal a patent: by whom it may be obtained; necessary instruments (memorial, summons, pleadings); evidence; new trial; judgment, costs; surrender and enrolment of vacatur; certificate of vacatur.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Scire facias is the statutory remedy to annul patents; the treatise details formal steps and evidentiary standards; the writ is generally directed to the sheriff of Middlesex and assembled in the petty bag office.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidence required in infringement actions (plaintiff's burden)
rubrics_metrics.description: Plaintiff must produce the exemplification of the letters patent and prove allegations: that the invention is new and useful, that he is the inventor, that the specification is sufficient, and that infringement occurred.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Proof of infringement may include inspection of manufactured articles, examination of factories (by court order), and comparison of specification with accused articles; adequate documentary proof of the patent and specification is required.

rubrics_metrics.name: Defendant's evidentiary defenses in infringement suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Defendant may show matters invalidating the patent: prior public use/publication, that the patentee was not the inventor, premeditated obscurity or concealment in the specification, and by comparison of the two manufactures.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Defendant can attack novelty, sufficiency of the specification, and entitlement; proof may include showing prior art, secret prior use, or that the specification was intended to mislead.

rubrics_metrics.name: Injunctions and equitable relief
rubrics_metrics.description: Injunctions may be granted to prevent infringement pending hearing and perpetual injunctions may be issued on grounds set out.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity practice includes filing bills, affidavits showing belief in original inventorship, motions for interim injunctions, answers, demurrers, feigned issues, factory inspections for evidence, and final equitable remedies including injunctions and accounts.

rubrics_metrics.name: What does not vitiate a patent
rubrics_metrics.description: The treatise enumerates circumstances that do not invalidate a patent generally.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Some irregularities or later discoveries may not automatically vitiate a patent; the text lists exceptions and nuances (see chapter on invalid patents and 'what things do not vitiate a patent'). Specifics depend on nature and context of the defect.

rubrics_metrics.name: Remedies and judgments in infringement suits
rubrics_metrics.description: Judgment effects in actions for infringement, including costs, damages, and the exercise of equitable jurisdiction.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise describes final judgments, interlocutory relief, costs awards, and judgment peculiarities on scire facias; no writ of error lies from judgment on a scire facias (procedural detail).

rubrics_metrics.name: Property in a patent (nature, duration, assignability)
rubrics_metrics.description: Property in a patent is personal in nature; its duration, number of interested persons, executors/administrators, assignees and mortgage/trust considerations are addressed.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Patents are assignable and subject to trusts/mortgages; statutory acts have enlarged terms/number of joint patentees; executors are treated as one person for interests; assignees of bankrupts and trusts have special treatment.

rubrics_metrics.name: Venue and parties for litigation
rubrics_metrics.description: Parties and venue rules: an assignee may sue alone or join; venue generally at Westminster; scire facias directed to sheriff of Middlesex.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Practical litigation rules are given for pleadings, venue selection, who may bring suits (including the crown and private subjects), and the pleadings and defences available in law and equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Feigned issues and trial practice in equity
rubrics_metrics.description: Use of feigned issues to try disputed facts (e.g., validity) in equity practice and resulting new trials.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Equity suits may direct feigned issues for jury trial on factual disputes; procedure and consequences (including new trials) are described in context of patent litigation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Models and forms
rubrics_metrics.description: Models and statutory/forms are collected in the Appendix and may be required/used in practice.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Models may be appended or required in practice; practitioners should consult the prescribed forms for petitions, bills, and enrolment procedures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limitations on the Crown's prerogative and historical policy
rubrics_metrics.description: The Crown's power to grant monopolies is limited by statute and policy; historical abuses led to statutory restraint (21 Jac. I.).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The treatise places patent law in historical context: monopolies at common law, historical grants, and restrictions imposed to protect trade and public interest; the statute is interpreted as declaratory of common law and as constraining arbitrary grants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Consequences of altering specification after sealing
rubrics_metrics.description: Alterations after patent sealed and use of cheaper materials/inadvertence have legal consequences.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Post-sealing changes may affect validity/enforceability; substituting cheaper materials or making inadvertent changes without proper disclosure can create problems—careful drafting and adherence to described embodiment is crucial.
